# Simulating Stopping Effects in Deformed Uranium Collisions

A Relativistic Transport Model (ART1.0) was employed to simulate the stopping effects arising in uranium-uranium (U+U) collisions at a beam kinetic energy of 520 MeV per nucleon. Owing to the pronounced quadrupole deformation of the uranium nucleus, two extreme collision geometries were considered in this study: the tip-tip configuration, in which the elongated axes of both nuclei are aligned along the beam direction, and the body-body configuration, in which these axes lie perpendicular to the beam. Comparing these orientations offers a valuable means of probing how the initial geometry of the colliding system influences the subsequent dynamics of the reaction.

The simulations demonstrate that central collisions in both extreme orientations are capable of achieving full nuclear stopping, thereby forming a bulk of hot, dense nuclear matter. Because the uranium nuclei are strongly deformed, the resulting fireball possesses a sufficiently large volume and a comparatively long lifetime. These conditions are particularly favorable for studying the properties of compressed nuclear matter, as they allow the system to reach and maintain equilibrium-like states over an extended spatial and temporal domain.

Distinct differences emerge in the collective flow observables between the two configurations. At normalized impact parameters below half the maximum value (b/b_max < 0.5), the nucleon sideward flow generated in tip-tip collisions is found to be nearly three times larger than that produced in body-body collisions. This substantial enhancement reflects the sensitivity of the sideward flow to the initial overlap geometry and to the pressure gradients developed within the compressed region.

The elliptic flow signal further distinguishes the two orientations. Body-body central collisions exhibit the largest negative nucleon elliptic flow, reaching a value of v₂ = −12%, which corresponds to a preferential emission of nucleons out of the reaction plane. In sharp contrast, tip-tip collisions yield essentially zero elliptic flow, a natural consequence of the azimuthal symmetry inherent to that particular geometry.

These findings carry direct relevance for forthcoming experimental efforts. The Cooling Storage Ring External Target Facility, to be constructed in Lanzhou, China, will deliver uranium beams at energies up to 520 MeV per nucleon. With its capability to explore precisely the collision systems examined in this work, the facility is expected to make significant contributions to constraining the nuclear equation of state and to advancing our understanding of the behavior of dense nuclear matter.

# Probing the Nuclear Equation of State with Uranium-Uranium Collisions

## Introduction

Understanding the properties of hot, dense nuclear matter remains one of the central goals of intermediate-energy heavy-ion physics. A key motivation is to constrain the nuclear equation of state (EOS), which governs the relationship between pressure, density, and temperature in nuclear systems and has profound implications for astrophysical phenomena such as neutron stars and supernova explosions. Deformed uranium nuclei offer a unique opportunity in this regard, because their strongly prolate shape allows experimentalists to create dramatically different initial geometries simply by selecting the relative orientation of the colliding nuclei.

In this work, a Relativistic Transport Model (ART1.0) was employed to simulate central U+U collisions at a beam energy of 520 MeV/nucleon. Two extreme configurations were considered: the tip-tip orientation, in which the long axes of both nuclei are aligned along the beam direction, and the body-body orientation, in which the long axes lie perpendicular to the beam and parallel to one another. By comparing these limiting geometries, we examine three observables—nuclear stopping, sideward (directed) flow, and elliptic flow—to assess their sensitivity as probes of the nuclear equation of state.

## Simulation Framework

The ART1.0 model is a hadronic transport approach that follows the propagation, scattering, and production of baryons and mesons throughout the collision. It incorporates mean-field potentials and a wide array of elastic and inelastic collision channels, making it well suited for describing the dynamics of nuclear matter at densities several times that of normal nuclear matter. The deformed density distributions of the uranium nuclei were initialized to reflect their prolate ground-state shapes, allowing the tip-tip and body-body orientations to be modeled with realistic geometric input.

## Nuclear Stopping

Nuclear stopping quantifies the degree to which the initial longitudinal motion of the colliding nucleons is converted into transverse and thermal motion, serving as a direct indicator of thermalization and energy deposition. The simulations reveal that both the tip-tip and body-body orientations achieve essentially full stopping at 520 MeV/nucleon. In each case, the incident nucleons are strongly decelerated and the available kinetic energy is efficiently redistributed, producing a highly excited, hot, and dense fireball. This confirms that the extreme uranium configurations are effective at forming the compressed nuclear matter necessary for EOS studies, regardless of orientation.

## Sideward Flow

Sideward, or directed, flow describes the collective deflection of nucleons within the reaction plane and is sensitive to the pressure gradients built up during the compression phase of the collision. The two orientations produce markedly different directed flow signatures. The tip-tip configuration exhibits nearly three times the sideward flow of the body-body configuration. This enhancement arises from the elongated overlap geometry along the beam axis, which produces a larger and more prolonged compression and thus stronger in-plane pressure gradients. The pronounced difference in directed flow between the two geometries highlights its usefulness as a discriminating observable for the stiffness of the equation of state.

## Elliptic Flow

Elliptic flow characterizes the anisotropy of particle emission in the plane transverse to the beam and is particularly sensitive to the interplay between the geometry of the participant region and the pressure that develops during the early, dense stage of the reaction. In the body-body orientation, the simulations yield a large negative elliptic flow of approximately −12%. This strongly negative value reflects a squeeze-out effect, in which nucleons are preferentially emitted out of the reaction plane because the elongated, bar-shaped overlap region and the surrounding spectator matter shadow in-plane emission. Such a distinctive and large elliptic-flow signal makes the body-body configuration an especially clean probe of the pressure and density conditions reached in the collision.

## Discussion and Outlook

Taken together, these results demonstrate that the extreme tip-tip and body-body orientations of U+U collisions provide complementary and highly sensitive probes of the nuclear equation of state. While both geometries reliably produce full stopping and form hot, dense nuclear matter, they generate qualitatively and quantitatively distinct collective-flow observables: the tip-tip configuration amplifies directed flow, whereas the body-body configuration produces a strong negative elliptic flow. By exploiting these controllable geometric extremes, experiments can isolate the effects of pressure and density on flow observables and thereby place tighter constraints on the EOS.

These findings are particularly timely in view of the upcoming CSR-ETF (Cooling Storage Ring–Experimental Terminal Facility), whose energy range and detection capabilities are well matched to the study of such collisions. The demonstrated sensitivity of sideward and elliptic flow to the collision orientation suggests that orientation-selected U+U measurements at CSR-ETF could offer a powerful experimental avenue for characterizing hot, dense nuclear matter and refining our understanding of the nuclear equation of state.

# Relativistic Transport Models

## Introduction

Relativistic transport models are theoretical frameworks used to describe the dynamical evolution of many-particle systems moving at velocities approaching the speed of light. These models play a central role in nuclear physics, astrophysics, and high-energy heavy-ion collision research, where particles are subjected to extreme conditions of temperature, density, and energy.

## Theoretical Foundation

At the heart of relativistic transport theory lies the challenge of reconciling classical kinetic descriptions with the principles of special relativity. Traditional transport equations, such as the Boltzmann equation, must be reformulated to remain covariant under Lorentz transformations. The result is the **relativistic Boltzmann equation**, which governs how the phase-space distribution function of particles evolves over time:

$$p^\mu \partial_\mu f(x, p) = C[f]$$

Here, the left-hand side describes the free-streaming motion of particles, while the collision term \( C[f] \) on the right accounts for interactions between particles. This formulation ensures that the transport dynamics are consistent with causality and the relativistic energy-momentum relationship.

## Key Applications

**Heavy-Ion Collisions:** One of the most prominent applications of relativistic transport models is in the study of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), a state of matter created in facilities such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Transport models help physicists interpret experimental observables like particle spectra, collective flow, and correlations.

**Nuclear Astrophysics:** These models are essential for understanding neutron stars, supernovae, and the behavior of dense nuclear matter under gravitational and electromagnetic forces.

**Non-Equilibrium Dynamics:** Relativistic transport models excel at describing systems far from thermal equilibrium, tracking how they evolve toward equilibrium through microscopic interactions.

## Common Modeling Approaches

Several established transport models are widely used in the scientific community:

- **BUU (Boltzmann–Uehling–Uhlenbeck) models**, which incorporate quantum statistical effects.
- **QMD (Quantum Molecular Dynamics)** approaches, which treat particles as localized wave packets.
- **Parton cascade models**, which describe the microscopic dynamics of quarks and gluons.

Each approach balances computational feasibility with physical accuracy, and the choice often depends on the specific phenomena under investigation.

## Conclusion

Relativistic transport models provide an indispensable bridge between fundamental theory and experimental observation. By capturing the complex interplay of relativistic kinematics and particle interactions, they enable researchers to probe the properties of matter under the most extreme conditions in the universe. As computational power and theoretical understanding continue to advance, these models will remain a cornerstone of modern high-energy and nuclear physics research.

We investigate nuclear stopping and collective flow phenomena in uranium-uranium (U+U) collisions at Cooling Storage Ring (CSR) energies using a relativistic transport model. Owing to the pronounced prolate deformation of the uranium nucleus, distinct collision geometries—namely tip-tip and body-body configurations—give rise to markedly different initial conditions in terms of participant density, geometric overlap, and energy deposition. We simulate these two extreme orientations to systematically explore how the initial spatial anisotropy influences the degree of nuclear stopping and the development of collective flow. Our results show that tip-tip collisions produce a more elongated and denser overlap region along the beam axis, leading to enhanced nuclear stopping as quantified by the rapidity distributions and stopping observables. In contrast, body-body collisions generate a larger transverse overlap area with stronger spatial eccentricity, resulting in more pronounced directed and elliptic flow signals. We analyze the rapidity dependence of the stopping power, the transverse momentum spectra, and the excitation functions of the flow coefficients ($v_1$ and $v_2$) for both configurations. The strong sensitivity of these observables to collision geometry demonstrates that orientation-selected U+U collisions provide a valuable tool for probing the equation of state and transport properties of the dense nuclear matter created at CSR energies. These findings offer theoretical guidance for forthcoming experimental measurements at CSR facilities.

# Abstract

Uranium-uranium collisions offer a unique opportunity to probe the nuclear equation of state (EoS) due to the pronounced prolate deformation of the ²³⁸U nucleus, which enables the study of collision geometry effects unattainable with spherical nuclei. In this work, we investigate nucleon sideward flow and elliptic flow in U+U collisions at energies relevant to the Cooling Storage Ring External-target Facility (CSR-ETF) in Lanzhou, focusing on two extreme collision orientations: tip-tip and body-body configurations.

Using transport model simulations, we demonstrate that the two geometries produce markedly different flow signatures. These orientation-dependent differences in the collective flow observables reflect the sensitivity of the emitted nucleons to both the density reached during the compression phase and the pressure gradients governing the subsequent expansion.

We argue that comparing flow observables between these limiting orientations provides a powerful differential constraint on the stiffness of the nuclear EoS, effectively varying the initial compression and geometry while holding the colliding system fixed. This approach reduces model dependencies inherent in comparisons across different collision systems. # Abstract

**Probing Dense Nuclear Matter through Configuration-Selected U+U Collisions: A Relativistic Transport Model Study**

The unique prolate deformation of the uranium nucleus offers a powerful tool for exploring the properties of dense nuclear matter under varying geometric conditions. In this work, we employ a relativistic transport model to systematically investigate central tip-tip and body-body configurations in U+U collisions at relativistic energies. By selecting extreme orientation configurations, we isolate the effects of initial geometry and overlap volume on the dynamical evolution of the produced medium. Our simulations reveal that tip-tip collisions generate systematically higher baryon and energy densities with extended lifetimes of the compressed phase compared to body-body collisions, owing to the elongated longitudinal overlap along the collision axis. In contrast, body-body configurations produce larger initial spatial eccentricities that translate into enhanced anisotropic collective flow. We quantify these differences through observables including the maximum central density, the space-time evolution of the high-density region, elliptic flow coefficients, and particle production yields. The results demonstrate that configuration-selected U+U collisions provide a sensitive experimental handle for disentangling density-driven from geometry-driven effects, thereby constraining the nuclear equation of state at supra-saturation densities. These findings underscore the potential of deformed-nucleus collisions as controlled probes of the QCD phase diagram and offer quantitative guidance for event-shape engineering in current and future heavy-ion experiments at facilities such as RHIC, FAIR, and NICA.

---

*Keywords: U+U collisions, nuclear deformation, relativistic transport model, dense nuclear matter, equation of state, collective flow*
